synonyms: Bothriochloa ischaemum var. songarica (Rupr. ex Fisch. & C.A.Mey.) Celarier & J.R.Harlan
Andropogon ischaemum var. songaricus Rupr. ex Fisch. & C.A.Mey.
taxonomic_note: Current Kew/POWO accepts Bothriochloa ischaemum at species rank and treats var. songarica, the Texas King Ranch bluestem name, as a synonym. Kew lists Texas as introduced, not native.
look_here_first: KR bluestem (introduced): look for several long, slender fingerlike flowering branches clustered together at the tip of a stem. Native little bluestem has shorter fuzzy flowering branches along separate upper stems.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO lists the native range in temperate Eurasia and northwestern Africa and explicitly lists Texas among introduced regions. Texas A&M AgriLife describes King Ranch bluestem as an introduced, aggressive warm-season perennial. Texas Invasives evaluates the songarica concept and documents strong impacts on native plant community richness, including near-monocultures.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Wild roadside or prairie occurrence in Texas does not count as native-range evidence.

morphology_keys.comparison_training: KR bluestem (*Bothriochloa ischaemum*, often locally called var. songarica): the terminal seedhead is a cluster of several relatively long, narrow spicate racemes, often 3–8; these may appear fingerlike or subdigitate. The central axis is commonly shorter than its racemes. Light green or straw culms often spread and kink at nodes. Stiff papilla-based hairs on the upper leaf surface just above the collar support identification. Little bluestem (*Schizachyrium scoparium*): a more distinct narrow perennial bunch. The upper culm divides into multiple leafy branches, with separate SHORT racemes at branch tips and from upper leaf sheaths, rather than all flowering branches gathering at one terminal center. Each raceme becomes silky/fluffy with mature seed; bluish green growing-season stems can redden, but color alone never proves species. CAUTION: do not tell crew that all KR bluestem nodes must be hairless. Texas A&M describes smooth nodes in its songarica treatment, while UT Austin local work (Bob Harms and Williamson County flora) describes short or appressed hairs. Node pubescence can vary among local/hybrid concepts and is not a safe single-character distinction. B. barbinodis, cane bluestem, has conspicuously BEARDED nodes; compare its heavier hair tufts separately.

advanced_confirmation.Leaf collar: On a confirmed same-plant specimen, inspect stiff papilla-based hairs on the upper leaf blade near the collar; photograph the true ligule with a ruler.
advanced_confirmation.Spikelet pairs: At 10–20× magnification, separate an attached sessile fertile spikelet from its pedicelled companion and check the awn; the current photos do not resolve this.
advanced_confirmation.Node-hair caution: Do NOT use hairless stem nodes as a required test. Texas A&M describes glabrous KR nodes, while local UT Austin treatments have noted short hairs. A heavy beard is useful when considering native cane bluestem.
advanced_confirmation.Native versus invasive decision: Use multiple characters and preserve the project's nonnative invasive-comparison status; never remove native bluestem on a seedhead silhouette alone.

comparisons.key_distinctions: KR bluestem (*Bothriochloa ischaemum*, often locally called var. songarica): the terminal seedhead is a cluster of several relatively long, narrow spicate racemes, often 3–8; these may appear fingerlike or subdigitate. The central axis is commonly shorter than its racemes. Light green or straw culms often spread and kink at nodes. Stiff papilla-based hairs on the upper leaf surface just above the collar support identification. Little bluestem (*Schizachyrium scoparium*): a more distinct narrow perennial bunch. The upper culm divides into multiple leafy branches, with separate SHORT racemes at branch tips and from upper leaf sheaths, rather than all flowering branches gathering at one terminal center. Each raceme becomes silky/fluffy with mature seed; bluish green growing-season stems can redden, but color alone never proves species. Kleberg bluestem (D. annulatum) can have a long spreading white ring at the true culm node and similar long terminal racemes; it overlaps KR panicle silhouette, so examine mature glumes/pedicelled partners and papilla-based KR blade hairs. Silky bluestem (D. sericeum) also has a conspicuous true nodal beard; white ring alone is NOT diagnostic of Kleberg.

field_sequence: 1. Stand back and photograph an ENTIRE rooted plant: KR may be sprawling and crowding neighbors; little bluestem generally forms a tighter persistent bunch.

2. Follow each flowering branch to its ORIGIN. KR: 3–8 or more relatively long racemes cluster near one terminal panicle center. Little: many short racemes distributed on different upper side branches.
3. Part an intact leaf sheath at the collar. Look for a small ligule and, on suspected KR, the stiff long papilla-based hairs on blade ABOVE the collar. Photograph at 10× with a mm reference.

4. Inspect 2–3 mature flowering units under a lens: their paired sessile fertile / pedicelled companion spikelets, bristles and bent/twisted awns. In little bluestem, check the short raceme's hairy axis segments and pedicel remnants.
5. If seedheads are absent or flowering-stage transitional, mark 'bluestem sp., KR suspected' rather than treating native *Schizachyrium* as an invasive.

lookalikes.cue: Native cane bluestem; conspicuous long beard of hairs at stem nodes and often a broader fanlike panicle. The BEARD is heavier than ordinary short hairs occasionally noted on KR.
Native silver bluestem; a dense cottony silvery head with many short fuzzy branches rather than KR's few longer slender fingers.

Introduced Kleberg bluestem; can have several fingerlike awned racemes and white-ringed nodes. Check leaf collar, node and mature spikelet morphology; do not classify every KR-looking grass from panicle alone.
Native bushy bluestem; a bulky brushy plume composed of crowded silky racemes, commonly in moist sites, unlike distributed short little-bluestem racemes.
Native little bluestem; distributed SHORT axillary/terminal racemes among numerous upper branches rather than a tight terminal cluster of LONG fingers.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Trace where EACH flowering raceme is attached to a leafy upper branch; then inspect the leaf sheath and blade collar.
field_matrix.kr_bluestem: Several elongated slender terminal fingers gathered at one panicle axis; stiff papilla-based hairs on the upper blade just above collar may be present.
field_matrix.look_alike: Many shorter separate silky racemes, usually one emerging from each upper leafy branch sheath; distinctive compressed/keeled basal sheaths and persistent tight bunch.
field_matrix.no_seedhead: Neither a spreading base nor smooth KR nodes are decisive. Check little bluestem keeled sheaths and KR possible papilla-based hairs near collar, then confirm after mature seedheads.
field_matrix.quick_rule: If your flowering culm has separate upper leafy branches each bearing its own short raceme, do NOT call it KR without stronger evidence.

field_matrix.taxon: Native cane, silver, bushy and big bluestems
field_matrix.where_to_look: Before KR removal, inspect node hairs and the structure of whole reproductive head.
field_matrix.kr_bluestem: Typically several LONG thin radiating terminal fingers with leaf collar hairs as support.
field_matrix.look_alike: Cane: heavy true node beard and broader fan. Silver: compact cottony many-short-rame plume. Bushy: dense spathe-associated cottony brush. Big: fewer stout turkey-foot fingers.
field_matrix.quick_rule: One detached fuzzy head or 3 terminal-looking branches cannot justify a KR removal.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Before treating terminal fingered heads as KR, inspect true culm nodes and upper blade collar on one whole, rooted flowering plant.
field_matrix.kr_bluestem: Similar few-to-many LONG slender terminal fingers. May show SHORT/appressed or absent node hairs; characteristic stiff papilla-based hairs above upper blade collar in local UT treatment.
field_matrix.look_alike: Kleberg may have LONG SPREADING white node hair rings and stoloniferous base. Similar terminal fingers; often more obtuse lower glume and long upper cilia on sessile spikelet.
field_matrix.how_to_decide: The head alone CANNOT cleanly separate. Compare true nodal ring, blade papilla hairs, mature glume apex and paired spikelet on same plant.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Silky may show white nodal beard and densely villous raceme clusters; compare with Kleberg and KR.
field_matrix.kr_bluestem: KR head branches group at one terminal point; papilla-based blade hairs at collar and mature glumes offer support.
field_matrix.look_alike: Dichanthium sericeum can have a large white nodal beard too; characteristic densely silky head plus mature sessile spikelet glumes needed.
field_matrix.how_to_decide: Do not trust hair-ring or head color alone; label introduced bluestem candidate if insufficient structures.

not_reliable_alone: Red, orange, bluish or tan leaf and stem color — weather, genetics and season cause overlap.
Fluffy white awned spikelets: several bluestems have them; trace WHERE flowering branches originate.
Size/height or tightly bunched appearance alone; mowing and drought alter both.
One smooth stem node on KR: some Hays-area variants have short appressed hairs; never enforce glabrous KR nodes.
A detached tuft of seedhead material that does not show its original attachment.
Source-labelled photo alone when it lacks the necessary anatomy.

field_id_finish_pass.kleberg_silky_crosscheck: KR and Kleberg share several terminal fingerlike racemes.
